concepts.title: The testing Package and *testing.T
concepts.description: Go bakes testing directly into its toolchain: a file ending in _test.go, a function named TestXxx taking a *testing.T, and the `go test` command are all you need -- no separate test runner or assertion library required, and understanding exactly how *testing.T reports failure versus stopping execution is the foundation every other testing concept builds on.
learningObjectives: Explain how `go test` discovers which files and functions to treat as tests, based on file and function naming conventions.
Write a test function with the correct signature and use *testing.T to report a failure without crashing the whole test binary.
Explain the difference between t.Error/t.Errorf and t.Fatal/t.Fatalf, and predict when using the wrong one hides a real bug or wastes a debugging session.
Use t.Helper() so failure line numbers point at the caller's line in the test, not at a line inside a shared helper function.
Explain why Go's standard library deliberately has no built-in assert function, and what idiom replaces it.

sections.heading: Test Discovery: File Names and Function Signatures Are the Whole Convention
*testing.T: Reporting a Failure Without Ending the Whole Suite
t.Helper(): Correct Line Numbers From Shared Assertion Code
No Built-In assert: A Deliberate Design Choice
sections.body:
Developers coming from languages or frameworks with a built-in `assert(condition)` -- one line, and it just works -- are often surprised that Go's standard `testing` package has nothing like it at all. This isn't an oversight; it follows directly from the same minimalism philosophy behind Go favoring small interfaces over frameworks (recall `io.Reader`/`io.Writer` from the Packages concept). An `assert`-style helper generally has to accept values of any type and compare them generically, which in Go historically meant leaning on `reflect.DeepEqual` or type-switching tricks to produce a readable failure message for arbitrary types -- machinery that adds indirection and can produce genuinely confusing failure messages (or, in some real-world assert libraries, quietly wrong comparisons for edge cases like comparing a `nil` slice to an empty one) compared to a plain `if` statement that says exactly what it means.

The idiomatic Go answer is simply: write an `if` statement, and call `t.Errorf`/`t.Fatalf` yourself with a clear, specific message when the condition you actually care about isn't met. This keeps every test's failure message under your own control, uses the language's own comparison and formatting operators (which you already understand precisely, with no library-specific quirks to learn), and avoids adding any dependency at all for something a four-line `if` block already does perfectly well. It's worth knowing that a genuinely popular third-party ecosystem (`testify`'s `assert`/`require` packages, for instance) exists and plenty of real Go codebases do use it for the more concise call sites it offers -- but the standard library and most of Go's own source tree deliberately stick to plain `if` + `t.Errorf`, and reading idiomatic Go test code fluently means being completely comfortable with that plainer style as the default, not the exception.

examples.title: A Minimal Test, and What go test Actually Prints
examples.explanation: Without `-v`, `go test` prints only a one-line summary per package -- `ok` and the elapsed time if every test passed, or `FAIL` with the specific failing test names' output if not -- deliberately terse so a healthy build produces minimal noise. `-v` (verbose) prints every test's name as it starts (`=== RUN`) and its individual result (`--- PASS` or `--- FAIL`) as it finishes, which is what you reach for while actively debugging a specific failing test rather than just checking whether the whole suite is green. Note that `TestAdd` never explicitly calls anything indicating success -- passing is simply the default outcome of a test function that runs to completion without ever calling `t.Error`, `t.Errorf`, `t.Fatal`, or `t.Fatalf`.

examples.title: t.Fatalf for a Precondition, t.Errorf for Independent Checks
examples.explanation: The error check uses `t.Fatalf` on purpose: if `ParseSettings` genuinely returned an error, `settings` is very likely a useless zero-value struct, and reading `settings.Timeout` or `settings.Retries` off it afterward would not tell you anything true about a bug in field-by-field parsing -- it would just report two more failures caused entirely by the first one, obscuring the actual root cause. The two field checks below it use `t.Errorf` deliberately, because they're genuinely independent of each other: if `Timeout` happens to be wrong, that tells you nothing about whether `Retries` is also wrong, so continuing to check `Retries` even after a `Timeout` failure gives you strictly more useful information in a single test run, rather than needing to fix one field and re-run just to discover the next one is also broken.

examples.title: t.Helper() Pointing Failures at the Real Call Site
examples.explanation: Because `assertEqual` calls `t.Helper()` as its very first line, a failure triggered by the third call reports itself as coming from line 14 -- the actual `assertEqual(t, Reverse("go"), "go")` call inside `TestReverse` -- rather than from the `t.Errorf` line inside `assertEqual` itself, which would be the same unhelpful line number no matter which of the three calls happened to fail. With three near-identical call sites in this test (and potentially dozens more across a real package), that distinction is what makes a failure immediately actionable versus requiring you to manually count which call must have triggered it. Removing the `t.Helper()` line wouldn't change whether the test correctly fails -- it only changes how quickly a person reading the failure output can find the actual problem.

misconceptions.description: Calling t.Fatal inside a test function stops the entire test binary immediately, so no other Test functions in the package will run after it.
misconceptions.clarification: t.Fatal (and t.FailNow, which it calls) only terminates the current test function's goroutine via runtime.Goexit -- it does not stop the test binary or skip any other TestXxx functions. go test continues on to run every other discovered test function in the package normally; only the one test function that called Fatal is cut short partway through its own body. Each TestXxx function gets this same independent treatment, which is exactly why one failing precondition in one test doesn't prevent you from seeing the pass/fail results of everything else in the same run.

misconceptions.description: Since Go's testing package has no built-in assert function, you can't write clear, readable tests without pulling in a third-party assertion library.
misconceptions.clarification: The standard, idiomatic pattern -- an ordinary if statement followed by t.Errorf or t.Fatalf with a message you write yourself -- is not a workaround or a lesser substitute; it is the pattern the standard library's own tests, and the overwhelming majority of production Go code, actually use. It requires no extra dependency, gives you full control over the exact failure message and comparison logic for every type you're testing, and avoids the genuinely real edge-case pitfalls that generic reflection-based comparison helpers can introduce (such as subtly different treatment of a nil slice versus an empty one). Third-party libraries like testify exist and are popular in some codebases for more concise call sites, but they are an added choice on top of a language that is already fully capable of clear, idiomatic testing with nothing beyond its own standard library.

exercises.prompt: What does `go test -v` print for this test, and does the overall test function pass or fail?
hints: t.Errorf records a failure and lets execution continue to the next line -- it does not stop the function the way t.Fatalf would.
Evaluate each if condition on its own: which of the three conditions is actually true, meaning its t.Errorf call never runs?
The overall test result (PASS or FAIL) depends on whether t.Error/t.Errorf was called at all during the run, even just once.
exercises.expectedAnswer: --- FAIL: TestValues, with two error messages printed: the first check's message (2+2 != 5 is true, so it fails and calls Errorf) and the third check's message (4+4 != 9 is true, so it also fails). The second check's condition (3+3 != 6) is false, so that Errorf never runs. The overall test is reported as FAIL because at least one Errorf was called, even though execution reached and completed all three if statements.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Each `if` is evaluated independently: `2+2 != 5` is true (4 != 5), so its Errorf fires and records message #1. `3+3 != 6` is false (6 == 6), so nothing happens on that line -- no message. `4+4 != 9` is true (8 != 9), so its Errorf fires and records message #2. Because t.Errorf never stops execution, all three if statements run regardless of what happened on the previous ones, which is why both failing checks get to report their own message in the same run, rather than the first failure hiding the second. The test function's overall status is FAIL the moment even one Errorf call happens anywhere during its execution, regardless of how many other checks in the same function happened to pass.

exercises.prompt: This test is meant to verify that a worker function correctly reports a failure via the test's *testing.T, but running it either hangs or produces a confusing panic instead of a clean, reported failure. Find and fix the bug.
hints: t.Fatal/t.Fatalf (and the FailNow method they call) are documented to work correctly only when called from the goroutine actually running the test function -- not from a goroutine the test itself spawned.
The failure check is currently running inside an anonymous goroutine started with `go func() { ... }()`, not directly inside TestProcessInvalidInput's own goroutine.

Change the failing check to use t.Errorf instead of t.Fatalf (safe from any goroutine), or restructure the code so the error is reported back to the main test goroutine and Fatalf/Errorf is called from there.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code called t.Fatalf from inside a goroutine spawned by the test itself, which the testing package explicitly documents as unsupported: FailNow (which Fatal/Fatalf call) is only meaningful when it can unwind the goroutine actually running the test function via runtime.Goexit -- calling it from a different goroutine cannot correctly stop that other goroutine's test function, and in practice tends to either hang (the done channel never gets closed because Goexit unwinds the spawned goroutine without running the rest of its deferred cleanup as expected relative to the test) or produce a confusing runtime panic instead of a clean, reported test failure. The fix moves the actual reporting call back into the test function's own goroutine: the spawned goroutine only computes and stores the result and error, and TestProcessInvalidInput itself -- after receiving from done -- performs the check and calls t.Fatalf from the correct goroutine, where FailNow behaves exactly as documented.

assessments.prompt: A test function has three independent checks in a row. Using t.Fatalf for the first check instead of t.Errorf would most likely cause which problem, assuming the first check happens to fail?
options: No difference at all -- Fatalf and Errorf always produce identical test output.
The entire test binary stops immediately, and no other TestXxx functions in the package run afterward.
The test function returns immediately after the first failure, so the second and third checks never run and never get a chance to report their own pass/fail status in this run.
Fatalf causes the test to be silently skipped rather than reported as failed.
assessments.explanation: t.Fatalf logs the failure and then stops executing the rest of that specific test function (via runtime.Goexit), so any checks written after it in the same function body never run during that test execution -- you'd only find out whether the second and third checks pass or fail on a later run, after fixing the first one. Option A is wrong because the whole point of Fatalf versus Errorf is that they behave differently in exactly this way. Option B is wrong -- Fatalf only affects the current test function, not the rest of the test binary or other TestXxx functions in the package. Option D is wrong -- Fatalf clearly marks the test as FAILED, not skipped; a skip is a distinct outcome produced by calling t.Skip, unrelated to Fatalf.

assessments.prompt: A _test.go file contains `func Testadd(t *testing.T) { ... }` -- note the lowercase 'a' immediately after 'Test'. What happens when `go test` runs?
options: go test fails to compile, reporting that Testadd is not a valid test function name.

Testadd is silently never discovered or run as a test at all -- it compiles fine as an ordinary, never-called function, and go test itself gives no error; only go vet might separately flag a possible malformed test function name.
go test automatically renames Testadd to TestAdd internally at compile time and runs it as a normal test.
Testadd runs normally, but any of its failures are reported without an associated test name, as an anonymous failure.
assessments.explanation: go test's discovery rule requires the character immediately after 'Test' to not begin with a lowercase letter; Testadd's lowercase 'a' means it simply doesn't match that shape, so it's treated as an ordinary function and never invoked by the test binary at all -- with zero error or warning from go build or go test themselves. go vet is a separate tool that can catch this specific case with a 'possible malformed name for test function' warning, but running go test alone gives no signal that an entire test was skipped. Option A is wrong -- this compiles without any error. Option C invents an auto-correction mechanism Go doesn't have. Option D is wrong because the function never runs at all, so there's no failure of any kind to report, named or anonymous.

assessments.prompt: A test spawns a goroutine with `go func() { ... }()`, and that goroutine calls `t.Fatalf(...)` when it detects a problem. What's the issue with this, according to this concept?
options: There is no issue -- t.Fatalf works correctly no matter which goroutine calls it.

t.Fatal/t.Fatalf (and the FailNow method they call) are documented to work correctly only when called from the goroutine that is actually running the test function itself; calling them from a separately spawned goroutine is a documented misuse that tends to hang the test or produce a confusing panic instead of a clean, reported failure.
t.Fatalf can only be called once per test function in total, regardless of which goroutine calls it, so this would fail on the second call.
This works correctly as long as the spawned goroutine is created before any t.Errorf call elsewhere in the same test function.
assessments.explanation: t.Fatal/t.Fatalf work by calling runtime.Goexit on the calling goroutine to unwind it -- but that mechanism can only correctly stop the specific goroutine that's actually running the test function. Called from a different, spawned goroutine, it cannot unwind the real test goroutine the way it's meant to, and in practice this tends to hang (if something is waiting on that spawned goroutine to signal completion, and Goexit prevents it from doing so as expected) or produce a confusing panic, rather than a clean, correctly-reported failure. Option A directly contradicts the documented restriction. Option C invents a call-count limit that doesn't exist. Option D is a red herring -- ordering relative to other Errorf calls has no bearing on this specific restriction.

assessments.prompt: A shared helper function `checkStatus(t *testing.T, got, want int)` is called from several different lines across multiple test functions in a package, and it does NOT call t.Helper(). When one particular call site triggers a failure via t.Errorf inside checkStatus, what line number does the test output report?
options: The line inside checkStatus itself where t.Errorf was called -- the same line number every time, regardless of which call site actually triggered it.
The exact call-site line that triggered the failure, since Go always attributes a failure to the original caller by default, with or without t.Helper().
No line number at all -- omitting t.Helper() suppresses line-number reporting entirely for any failure that flows through that helper.
A line number chosen arbitrarily among all the call sites that use this helper, to encourage developers to add t.Helper().
assessments.explanation: Without t.Helper() marking the helper function, a failure reported from inside it points at the line inside the helper where t.Errorf/t.Fatalf was actually called -- the same generic line number no matter which of the many call sites across the package actually triggered that particular failure. This is precisely the problem t.Helper() exists to fix: calling it makes the testing package instead attribute the failure to the nearest calling line that isn't itself marked as a helper, which is the actual, specific call site a developer needs to look at. Option B describes t.Helper()'s effect, not the default behavior without it. Option C and D both invent behaviors -- suppressed reporting, or arbitrary attribution -- that aren't how this actually works; the default behavior is simply to always report the helper's own internal line.

assessments.prompt: Explain why Go's testing package provides no built-in assert function, and what happens to a test's usefulness if a shared assertion helper function forgets to call t.Helper().
assessments.modelAnswer: Go's testing package deliberately omits a generic assert(condition) helper for the same underlying reason the language favors small, explicit tools over larger abstracting frameworks elsewhere in the standard library: a generic assertion helper that works across arbitrary types typically has to lean on reflection-based comparison (like reflect.DeepEqual) to produce any kind of readable failure message, which adds indirection, can behave subtly differently than you'd expect on certain edge cases (such as comparing a nil slice to an empty one), and hides the exact comparison logic behind someone else's implementation rather than your own explicit if statement. The idiomatic replacement is simply to write the comparison yourself with an ordinary if, and call t.Errorf or t.Fatalf with a specific, hand-written message when the condition you actually care about isn't satisfied -- which costs a few extra lines per check but keeps every failure message, and the exact semantics of every comparison, fully under the test author's control and readable without needing to know any assertion library's particular conventions. As for t.Helper(): forgetting to call it inside a shared helper function doesn't break the test's correctness at all -- a failing check still correctly marks the test as FAILED -- but it does degrade the failure report's usefulness, because without it, the reported file and line number point at the line inside the shared helper where t.Errorf/t.Fatalf was actually called, rather than at whichever of the (often many) call sites in the actual test function triggered that particular failure. In a package with a helper used across dozens of call sites, that missing t.Helper() call is the difference between immediately knowing which specific assertion failed and having to manually narrow it down by inspection or by temporarily commenting out call sites.

concepts.title: Table-Driven Tests
concepts.description: Table-driven tests are Go's idiomatic answer to testing many input/output cases without duplicating the same test logic over and over: a slice (or map) of named cases, run through t.Run subtests, so each case gets its own isolated pass/fail result and its own selectable name in go test output.
learningObjectives: Explain what a table-driven test is and why it avoids duplicating test logic across many structurally similar test cases.
Write a table-driven test using a slice of structs with named fields for input, expected output, and a case name.
Use t.Run to create named subtests, and explain what isolation and selective execution it provides that a plain loop with t.Errorf does not.
Explain the loop-variable-capture bug that appears when a table-driven test uses t.Parallel(), and how to avoid it (or why Go 1.22+ removes the need to).
Design test case names that make a failing subtest immediately diagnosable from go test -v output alone, without opening the source file.

sections.heading: The Problem Table-Driven Tests Solve
sections.body:
Imagine testing a function like `IsPalindrome(s string) bool` against a dozen different inputs: empty string, single character, a real palindrome, a non-palindrome, mixed case, one with punctuation. The naive approach is to write a separate `TestIsPalindromeEmpty`, `TestIsPalindromeSingleChar`, `TestIsPalindromeReal`, and so on -- each one nearly identical except for the specific input and expected result. This duplicates the actual comparison-and-report logic across every single test function, which means any improvement to how failures are reported (a better message format, an added edge case check) has to be copy-pasted into every one of those near-identical functions, and it's easy for them to drift out of sync with each other over time.

**Table-driven testing** inverts this: write the comparison-and-report logic exactly once, and drive it from a **table** -- a plain Go data structure, almost always a slice of structs -- listing every case you want to check. Adding a new case becomes a one-line addition to the table, not a new function; the actual test logic is reviewed and gets better exactly once, for every case at once, instead of once per copy-pasted function. This is such a dominant idiom in real Go code that seeing a table literal immediately followed by a loop and `t.Run` is close to a universal signal, in any unfamiliar Go codebase, that you're looking at a test file.

sections.heading: The Table: A Slice of Named Cases
t.Run: Naming, Isolating, and Selecting Subtests
sections.body: `t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T) {...})` does three genuinely distinct, useful things, none of which a plain `for` loop calling `t.Errorf` directly (without `t.Run`) would give you. First, **naming**: each subtest's name shows up in `go test -v` output as `TestIsPalindrome/empty_string`, `TestIsPalindrome/simple_palindrome`, and so on (spaces in names are replaced with underscores) -- immediately identifying which specific case passed or failed. Second, **isolation**: `t.Run`'s callback receives its **own**, distinct `*testing.T`, separate from the outer one -- which means a `t.Fatalf` call inside one subtest only terminates that one subtest, not the entire `TestIsPalindrome` function; every other case in the table still runs to completion and reports its own result, exactly as if each had been a fully separate top-level `TestXxx` function. Without `t.Run` -- just calling `t.Fatalf` directly inside the loop body -- a single fatal case would abort every remaining case in the table, silently hiding whatever those later cases might have told you. Third, **selective execution**: `go test -run 'TestIsPalindrome/simple_palindrome'` runs only that one named subtest, which is invaluable while iterating on a fix for one specific failing case without re-running (and waiting on) the entire table every time.

sections.heading: The t.Parallel Loop-Variable Trap

examples.title: A Table-Driven Test for a Pure Function
examples.explanation: Each entry in `cases` fully describes one scenario: a human-readable `name`, the `input` fed to `Abs`, and the `want` result. The loop's only job is mechanical -- call `Abs`, compare, report -- and that logic is written exactly once regardless of how many cases the table eventually grows to. The `-v` output shows each subtest nested under the parent `TestAbs`, with its own PASS/FAIL line, giving an immediate, readable breakdown of exactly which named scenario succeeded, without needing to infer anything from a case index or from reading the table's source order.

examples.title: A Table Including Expected Errors
examples.explanation: Adding a `wantErr bool` field to the table lets a single table cover both success and failure scenarios for the same function, which is an extremely common real-world shape for input-validation code. The `t.Fatalf` inside this subtest is deliberate and safe here: because it's inside a `t.Run` callback, a fatal mismatch on the error-presence check only stops that one subtest -- the other three cases in the table still run and report independently. The second check (`err == nil && got != tc.want`) only even attempts to compare `got` when there genuinely was no error, avoiding a comparison against a `got` value that's meaningless whenever `ParsePort` legitimately failed.

examples.title: The t.Parallel Loop-Capture Bug, and the Explicit Fix
examples.explanation: In the vulnerable version, `t.Parallel()` tells the enclosing loop to move on to the next `tc` immediately, deferring this subtest's actual body until later, once the parent test reaches the point where it waits for all parallel subtests to finish. On Go versions before 1.22, there is only one `tc` variable for the whole loop, so by the time any of the parallel subtests actually execute their bodies, they're all very likely reading the table's final entry -- exactly the goroutine-closure bug from the Concurrency module, just triggered through t.Parallel() instead of a bare `go` statement. The fixed version's `tc := tc` line creates a new, independent variable, scoped to that specific loop iteration, that the subtest closure captures instead of the shared loop variable -- this line is a no-op in the sense that Go 1.22+ already gives each iteration its own `tc` automatically, but writing it explicitly keeps the test correct on any Go version and signals the author's intent clearly to any reader, regardless of which Go version they have in mind.

misconceptions.description: Since all the subtests in a table-driven test share the outer TestXxx function's *testing.T, calling t.Fatalf inside one subtest's t.Run callback stops every remaining case in the table from running.
misconceptions.clarification: Each call to t.Run passes its callback a brand-new, distinct *testing.T value, separate from the outer test's own *testing.T and from every other subtest's. A t.Fatalf call inside one subtest's callback only terminates that specific subtest -- via runtime.Goexit on that subtest's own goroutine -- and has no effect on any other t.Run call in the same loop; every other table entry still runs to completion and reports its own independent pass or fail result, exactly as if each subtest were its own separate top-level test function.

misconceptions.description: Once a codebase is confirmed to be running Go 1.22 or later, the classic t.Parallel loop-variable bug in table-driven tests is entirely a non-issue and can be forgotten about.
misconceptions.clarification: Go 1.22 does fix the underlying cause at the language level -- each loop iteration now gets its own independent copy of the range variable -- so newly written code on 1.22+ is genuinely safe without any extra shadowing line. But real codebases are rarely monolithically on one Go version forever: code gets copied between projects with different go.mod language versions, tutorials and blog posts referencing older idioms circulate for years, and a team member reading unfamiliar table-driven test code has no way to visually tell which Go version's semantics apply just by looking at the loop. Writing the explicit `tc := tc` shadow (or passing tc as an explicit parameter) costs one line and keeps the test's correctness independent of which Go version happens to compile it -- treating the 1.22 fix as a reason to stop writing defensively, rather than as a safety net underneath already-correct code, trades a small amount of clarity for a subtle version-dependence that's easy to forget about later.

exercises.prompt: Given this table-driven test, what does `go test -v` print, and which specific subtest (by name) fails?
hints: Each case runs as its own named subtest via t.Run -- work through each one's want value against what Capitalize would actually and correctly return.
The first two cases have entirely plausible want values that match what a correct Capitalize implementation should produce.

The third case's want value, "X", doesn't match what the comment says a correct Capitalize("") actually returns -- that mismatch is the deliberately introduced bug in the TEST, not necessarily in Capitalize itself.
exercises.expectedAnswer: TestCapitalize/lowercase_word and TestCapitalize/already_capitalized both PASS. TestCapitalize/empty_string FAILS, reporting something like 'Capitalize("") = "", want "X"'. The overall TestCapitalize is reported as FAIL because at least one of its subtests failed, even though two of the three passed.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The first case expects Capitalize("hello") to be "Hello", which matches correct capitalization behavior, so it passes. The second case expects Capitalize("World") to remain "World" (already capitalized), which also matches correct behavior and passes. The third case expects Capitalize("") to equal "X", but a correct Capitalize implementation applied to an empty string has nothing to capitalize and returns "" -- so got ("") does not equal want ("X"), and this subtest's t.Errorf fires, reporting the mismatch with the actual and wrong-expected values. Because t.Run gives each case its own independent *testing.T, the failing third case has no effect on the first two, which is why they still report PASS in the same run; the parent TestCapitalize is marked FAIL overall simply because at least one of its subtests failed, following the general rule that a test function fails if any Error/Errorf/Fatal/Fatalf fired anywhere within its own run, including within any of its subtests.

exercises.prompt: This table-driven test is supposed to check three cases in parallel, but on older Go versions (and unreliably even on some newer ones, depending on toolchain settings) all three subtests report the SAME result -- as if they all tested the third case's input, `"ccc"`. Find and fix the bug.
hints: t.Parallel() defers this subtest's actual execution -- the loop moves on to the next case immediately rather than waiting for this subtest's body to run first.

Because the loop keeps advancing without waiting, by the time any of the parallel subtests actually run their bodies, the shared loop variable tc may have already moved on to (or past) the table's last entry.

Shadow tc inside the loop body -- `tc := tc` -- immediately before the t.Run call, so each subtest closure captures its own independent copy of that iteration's case, not the one shared loop variable.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because `t.Parallel()` is called inside each subtest, that subtest pauses and hands control back to the loop immediately, rather than running its body right away -- the loop reaches all three t.Run calls, and only afterward do the parallel subtests actually execute, once the parent test function finishes and waits for them. On a Go version (or toolchain configuration) without per-iteration loop variables, there is only one shared `tc`, so by the time any subtest's deferred body actually runs, `tc` typically holds the table's last entry (`{name: "case c", input: "ccc", want: 0}`) for all three -- which is exactly why every subtest appeared to test `"ccc"`, even the ones named "case a" and "case b". The fix, `tc := tc` immediately inside the loop body before `t.Run`, declares a brand-new variable scoped to that single iteration, which the subtest's closure then captures instead of the shared loop variable -- giving each of the three subtests its own, correctly distinct case data regardless of when its deferred body actually executes.

assessments.prompt: What is the primary benefit t.Run provides over simply looping through a table of cases and calling t.Errorf directly inside the loop, with no t.Run at all?
options: t.Run makes each case's checks run measurably faster than a plain loop, even without calling t.Parallel().

t.Run gives each case its own independent *testing.T, so a case's name appears in -v output, a t.Fatalf in one case only stops that case (not the whole table), and individual cases become selectable via go test -run.
t.Run is required by the Go compiler -- a for loop calling t.Errorf directly without t.Run does not compile.
t.Run automatically deduplicates table entries that happen to have identical input values.
assessments.explanation: t.Run's real value is isolation, naming, and selectability: each call gets its own *testing.T (so a Fatalf in one case doesn't abort the rest of the table), each case's name becomes part of the subtest's identity in -v output and in go test -run patterns, and cases can be run individually while debugging. Option A is wrong -- t.Run alone provides no speed benefit; concurrency only happens if you additionally call t.Parallel() inside the callback. Option C is wrong -- a plain loop with t.Errorf and no t.Run compiles and runs fine; it just loses the isolation/naming/selection benefits, and a Fatalf in it would abort the entire remaining table rather than just one case. Option D is wrong -- there's no deduplication behavior in t.Run at all; duplicate-content cases simply both run and both report under their own (or, if truly identical, disambiguated) names.

assessments.prompt: A table-driven test uses `cases := map[string]struct{ input string; want bool }{...}` instead of a slice, with each map key doubling as the case's name. Which of these is a genuine consequence of this choice, according to this concept?
options: Case names must be numeric, since Go always converts map keys used as test names into their index position within the map.

Iterating the map to drive t.Run executes the cases in a randomized order on every run (Go's map iteration order is intentionally randomized), and if two entries accidentally share the same key, the later one silently overwrites the earlier one rather than producing two distinct cases.
Map-based tables run measurably faster overall than slice-based tables, because maps provide O(1) lookup for each case during the loop.
t.Run cannot accept a case name derived from a map key -- its name argument only accepts string literals known at compile time.
assessments.explanation: Using a map for the table has two genuine, specific consequences: because Go deliberately randomizes map iteration order, the cases run in a different order on each invocation of go test, which can be a deliberate feature for catching order-dependent bugs; and because map keys must be unique, an accidentally duplicated key doesn't produce two cases -- it silently collapses down to just the later entry, since it overwrites the earlier one in the map itself. Option A invents a numeric-conversion rule that doesn't exist -- map keys are used as-is for the case name. Option C overstates the performance angle; the loop still iterates once per case either way, and lookup speed isn't the relevant cost here. Option D is wrong -- t.Run's name parameter is an ordinary string value, computed however you like, including from a loop variable holding a map key.

assessments.prompt: A table-driven test loops over cases and calls `t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {...})` for each one, but never calls t.Parallel() inside the callback, on a Go version before 1.22. Is this specific test vulnerable to the classic loop-variable-capture bug, where every subtest ends up seeing the same, final tc?
options: Yes -- any closure created inside a for loop, parallel or not, has always been vulnerable to this bug on every Go version before 1.22.

No -- without t.Parallel(), t.Run is synchronous and blocks until the subtest's callback fully returns before the loop advances to the next tc, so the closure always reads the correct, current-iteration tc; the bug only appears once t.Parallel() causes the subtest's body to be deferred until after the loop has already moved on.
Yes, but only once the table grows past a certain number of cases.
No, but only because table-driven tests are required to declare `tc := tc` by the Go compiler whenever t.Run is used.
assessments.explanation: t.Run without a subsequent t.Parallel() call runs its callback synchronously -- the loop does not advance to the next case until the current subtest's entire callback has finished executing, which means the closure inside it always observes the correct tc for that specific iteration, entirely independent of which Go version is in use. The bug is specifically introduced by t.Parallel(), which pauses the subtest and returns control to the loop immediately, deferring the actual body until later, which is when the pre-1.22 shared-loop-variable problem can actually manifest. Option A overstates the vulnerability -- synchronous t.Run was never affected, on any Go version. Option C invents a scale-dependent threshold that doesn't exist. Option D invents a compiler-enforced requirement; `tc := tc` is a manual convention, never something the compiler mandates.

assessments.prompt: TestParsePort has four named subtests: "valid port", "empty string", "non-numeric", and "negative number". Which command runs only the "non-numeric" subtest, skipping the other three?
options: go test -run 'TestParsePort/non-numeric'
go test -subtest 'non-numeric'
go test -bench 'TestParsePort/non-numeric'
It isn't possible to select a single named subtest in isolation -- go test -run only ever matches against top-level TestXxx function names, never individual subtests.
assessments.explanation: go test -run takes a regular expression matched against the full subtest path, where a slash separates the parent test's name from each subtest's name -- 'TestParsePort/non-numeric' selects exactly that one subtest, leaving the other three in the table unrun for this invocation. This is precisely the selective-execution benefit t.Run provides over a plain loop with no subtests at all. Option B invents a flag (-subtest) that doesn't exist in the standard toolchain. Option C is wrong -- -bench is for running BenchmarkXxx functions, an entirely separate mechanism from ordinary tests. Option D is incorrect -- -run's pattern matching explicitly supports the slash-separated subtest-path syntax used in option A.

assessments.prompt: Explain why table-driven tests are considered idiomatic in Go, and walk through exactly what goes wrong -- and why -- if a table-driven test's subtests call t.Parallel() without properly scoping the loop variable on a Go version before 1.22.
assessments.modelAnswer: Table-driven tests are idiomatic because they separate 'what to check' from 'how to check it': the table is a plain slice (or map) of named cases -- each just data, with a name and whatever inputs and expected outputs the scenario needs -- while the actual comparison-and-report logic is written exactly once, in a loop, driving every case through it. This means growing test coverage for a function is usually a one-line addition to the table rather than a new, nearly-duplicate test function, and any improvement to how failures are reported benefits every case simultaneously rather than needing to be copy-pasted across many near-identical functions. Wrapping each case in t.Run further improves this by giving each case its own name in test output, its own independent *testing.T (so a fatal failure in one case doesn't prevent the rest of the table from running and reporting), and the ability to re-run just one named case while debugging, via go test -run. The t.Parallel bug is a direct consequence of what t.Parallel() actually does: rather than running the subtest's body immediately, it pauses that subtest and returns control to the surrounding loop right away, deferring the actual body until later, once the parent test reaches the point where it waits on all its parallel children. On a Go version before 1.22, a for loop reuses one single loop variable across every iteration rather than creating a fresh one per iteration -- so every parallel subtest's closure, when it finally does run later, is reading that one shared variable, which by then typically holds the table's very last entry, since the loop itself finished advancing through all the entries well before any parallel subtest got around to actually executing. The practical effect is that every subtest silently ends up testing the last case's data instead of its own, usually producing either an oddly uniform set of pass/fail results or several confusingly identical failure messages that don't match each subtest's own name. Go 1.22 fixes this by specifying that each loop iteration gets its own independent copy of the range variable, so this exact code becomes correct without any change -- but the classic, version-independent fix, explicitly shadowing the variable with `tc := tc` inside the loop body before calling t.Run, remains good practice specifically because it makes the code correct and self-evidently so regardless of which Go version eventually compiles it.

concepts.title: Benchmarks with testing.B
concepts.description: The testing package extends past correctness checks into performance measurement: a BenchmarkXxx function driven by *testing.B and its self-calibrating b.N loop counter lets you measure real execution time and allocations, but only if you understand exactly what the compiler is and isn't allowed to optimize away.
learningObjectives: Write a benchmark function with the correct signature, and explain what b.N represents and why the testing framework -- not you -- chooses its value.
Run benchmarks with go test -bench and interpret the ns/op (and, with -benchmem, B/op and allocs/op) output.
Explain why a benchmarked call whose result is never used can be optimized away by the compiler, producing a misleadingly fast measurement, and how the package-level sink pattern prevents it.
Use b.ResetTimer (and b.StopTimer/b.StartTimer) to exclude expensive one-time setup work from a benchmark's measured time.
Explain why hardcoding the loop bound instead of using b.N defeats the framework's calibration and produces unreliable, non-comparable measurements.

sections.heading: The Benchmark Signature and b.N: A Loop You Write, a Count You Don't Choose
Running Benchmarks and Reading the Numbers
sections.body:
Benchmarks don't run by default with a plain `go test` -- you opt in with the `-bench` flag, which takes a regular expression matched against benchmark names (`-bench=.` matches everything). A subtlety worth knowing: `go test` by default *also* runs every regular `TestXxx` function in the package even when you only asked for benchmarks, which is often not what you want while specifically iterating on performance -- the common idiom to skip tests entirely is `-run=^$` (a regular expression matching no test name at all), combined with `-bench`:

```
$ go test -bench=. -run=^$
goos: linux
goarch: amd64
pkg: example.com/mathutil
BenchmarkFibonacci10-8      5000000               243 ns/op
PASS
ok      example.com/mathutil    1.360s
```

The `-8` suffix on the benchmark name reflects `GOMAXPROCS` at the time of the run (recall from the Concurrency module that this is the number of OS threads the Go runtime will use). `5000000` is the final, calibrated `b.N` the runner settled on. `243 ns/op` is the actual measurement: total elapsed time for the loop, divided by `b.N` -- the average nanoseconds per single call to whatever's inside the loop. Adding `-benchmem` reports two more columns, `B/op` (bytes allocated per operation) and `allocs/op` (number of distinct heap allocations per operation) -- often at least as useful as raw speed, since allocation count is frequently the real lever behind a slow function, and it's a number that doesn't vary from run to run nearly as much as timing does, making it a more stable metric for comparing two implementations.

sections.heading: The Dead-Code-Elimination Trap: When a Benchmark Measures Nothing
Excluding Setup Cost: ResetTimer, StopTimer, StartTimer

examples.title: A Basic Benchmark and Its -benchmem Output
examples.explanation: Both benchmarks measure a tiny operation many times, and the -benchmem columns tell a more useful story than raw speed alone would: string concatenation with the `+` operator on constant strings here allocates nothing at all (the Go compiler can constant-fold or otherwise avoid heap allocation for this specific pattern), while `fmt.Sprintf` -- which has to do genuine runtime formatting work, including allocating a new string for its result -- performs 2 allocations and 32 bytes per call. In a hot code path called millions of times, that per-call allocation difference compounds into real, measurable garbage-collector pressure, which is exactly the kind of thing `-benchmem` surfaces that a pure timing number can obscure -- two implementations can have similar ns/op while one quietly allocates far more.

examples.title: Preventing Dead-Code Elimination With a Package-Level Sink
examples.explanation: `BenchmarkFibBad` calls `fib(20)` purely for its computational cost and never reads the return value at all -- across different Go compiler versions and optimization levels, this is exactly the shape of code that has, in real documented cases, ended up partially or fully elided, producing a benchmark number far faster than the function could plausibly run if its result actually mattered anywhere. `BenchmarkFibGood` restructures the same work so that the result flows into `r` on every iteration and then into the package-level `sink` once at the end -- since `sink` is a package-level variable, the compiler cannot prove nothing outside this function will ever read it, so it cannot justify skipping the computation that produces its value. The lesson generalizes beyond this specific fib example: any time a benchmark's inner loop computes a value and then does nothing else with it, that's worth a second look before trusting the reported number.

examples.title: Excluding Expensive Setup With b.ResetTimer
examples.explanation: `buildSortedSlice(1_000_000)` allocates and fills a million-element slice -- genuinely slow relative to a single binary search, and completely beside the point of a benchmark whose entire purpose is measuring `sort.SearchInts` itself. Without `b.ResetTimer()`, that setup cost would be folded into the very first calibration run's elapsed time (and, more subtly, get re-paid on every calibration re-run of the whole function, since setup sits outside the b.N loop but inside the function body), inflating and distorting the reported ns/op in a way that has nothing to do with the search algorithm's actual per-call cost. Calling `b.ResetTimer()` immediately after setup and immediately before the loop zeroes out everything measured so far, so the final reported number reflects only the cost of the `b.N` search calls themselves.

misconceptions.description: b.N is a fixed value (like 1000000) that you can rely on always being the same across runs and machines, so it's safe to write benchmark logic that assumes a specific magnitude for it.
misconceptions.clarification: b.N is chosen dynamically by the testing package's benchmark runner, separately for every single run, based on how long your loop body actually takes to execute on that specific machine at that specific moment -- a fast operation gets a much larger b.N (to accumulate enough total elapsed time for a stable measurement) than a slow one does, and the exact same benchmark can land on meaningfully different b.N values across different machines, different Go versions, or even different runs on the same machine under different load. Benchmark code must never assume any particular magnitude for b.N -- the entire design point of leaving it to the framework is that you shouldn't have to guess a 'good enough' iteration count yourself.

misconceptions.description: A benchmark reporting an extremely low ns/op compared to what you'd intuitively expect is good news -- it means the code under test is exceptionally fast.
misconceptions.clarification: An implausibly fast result is frequently a red flag, not a win: it can indicate that the compiler determined the computed result was never actually used anywhere and eliminated some or all of the real work as dead code, meaning the benchmark measured little or nothing close to the operation you intended to measure. Before trusting a suspiciously fast number, check whether the benchmark's result ever flows somewhere the compiler can't prove is unreachable -- typically a package-level sink variable assigned at the end of the benchmark function -- rather than treating an unexpectedly tiny ns/op as confirmation of a great implementation.

exercises.prompt: Two benchmarks are written to measure the same underlying function, `hash(data []byte) uint64`, which does real, non-trivial work. One of them is very likely to report a suspiciously, implausibly fast ns/op compared to the other. Which one, and why?
hints: Look at what happens to hash(data)'s return value in each loop body -- is it captured anywhere, or is the call made purely for its side effect on the CPU?
A compiler is permitted to eliminate work whose result it can prove is never observed by anything. Which of these two loops gives the compiler that kind of proof opportunity?
The sink pattern -- assigning the final result to a package-level variable -- exists specifically to deny the compiler that opportunity.
exercises.expectedAnswer: BenchmarkHashA is the one likely to report a suspiciously fast, unreliable ns/op. Its loop calls hash(data) and discards the result every iteration, giving the compiler a potential opportunity to determine the call's result (and possibly the call itself, depending on inlining and optimization) is never used and eliminate some of that work. BenchmarkHashB assigns the result to r each iteration and then to the package-level sink at the end, which the compiler cannot prove is unused, so it must actually perform the real work every time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: BenchmarkHashA's loop body is `hash(data)` with the return value completely discarded -- nothing in the function ever reads what hash returns. This is exactly the shape of code vulnerable to dead-code elimination: since the result is provably never observed by anything, an optimizing compiler is permitted, in principle, to skip performing (some or all of) the actual computation, especially if hash is small enough to be inlined at the call site, removing the function-call boundary that would otherwise obscure this from the compiler. BenchmarkHashB avoids this by capturing the result in a loop-local r on every iteration and then writing r into the package-level sink variable once, after the loop -- because sink is a package-level variable, the compiler has no way to prove nothing outside this function will ever read its value, so it cannot justify eliminating the work that produces it. If BenchmarkHashA reports a dramatically lower ns/op than BenchmarkHashB for what should be the identical underlying computation, that gap itself is strong evidence of exactly this kind of unintended optimization, not evidence that hash is somehow faster when called from HashA.

exercises.prompt: This benchmark is supposed to let go test's benchmark runner calibrate how many iterations to run for a stable measurement, but every run reports wildly different, noisy numbers and never seems to run long enough to stabilize. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Compare the loop bound used here to the identifier the testing package expects a benchmark to loop up to.

The benchmark runner calibrates by re-running your ENTIRE function with successively larger b.N values until the elapsed time is stable -- but this loop's bound never changes no matter what b.N the runner decides on.
Change the hardcoded 100 to b.N, so each calibration re-run actually executes as many iterations as the runner has decided to try this time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original loop always runs exactly 100 iterations, completely ignoring b.N -- so no matter what iteration count the benchmark runner decides to try during its calibration process, this function always does the same fixed, tiny amount of work, and the resulting elapsed time is dominated by measurement noise (timer resolution, scheduling jitter) rather than by Factorial's actual per-call cost, which is exactly why the reported numbers vary wildly and never settle down. The fix replaces the hardcoded `100` with `b.N`: now, when the runner tries a larger N to get a longer, more stable total measurement, the loop actually performs that many iterations, letting the elapsed-time-divided-by-N calculation converge on a meaningful, low-noise ns/op value instead of being swamped by fixed per-run overhead.

assessments.prompt: Why does a benchmark function write its own loop as `for i := 0; i < b.N; i++` instead of the testing package simply calling the benchmark function b.N separate times itself?
options: Writing the loop yourself lets you include one-time setup code (outside the loop) that shouldn't be repeated on every iteration, while still letting the framework control exactly how many timed iterations of the actual operation occur.
It is purely a stylistic convention with no functional difference from the framework calling the function N times directly.
b.N loops are required because Go does not support passing a function as an argument to be called multiple times.
Writing your own loop is necessary only when using -benchmem; plain timing benchmarks never need an explicit loop.
assessments.explanation: Writing the loop inside your own function is what lets you place expensive one-time setup (building test data, opening a resource) before the loop, where it happens exactly once per calibration attempt, while the loop itself repeats only the specific operation you actually want measured, exactly b.N times, whatever the runner decides that should be for this run. If the framework instead called your function N separate times, any setup code inside it would also run N times, making it effectively impossible to separate one-time cost from per-operation cost within a single benchmark function. Option B undersells a real functional distinction. Option C is incorrect -- Go fully supports passing and calling functions as values, unrelated to why benchmarks are structured this way. Option D is incorrect -- the b.N loop is required for every benchmark regardless of whether -benchmem is used; -benchmem simply adds allocation-tracking columns to output that already depends on the same loop structure.

assessments.prompt: Running `go test -bench=. -run=^$` prints `BenchmarkFibonacci10-8   5000000   243 ns/op`. What do the `-8` suffix and the `5000000` figure each represent?
options: -8 is this benchmark's ID number among all benchmarks that ran; 5000000 is the total number of nanoseconds elapsed across the entire run.
-8 reflects GOMAXPROCS at the time of the run (the number of OS threads the Go runtime will use); 5000000 is the final, calibrated b.N value the runner settled on for this benchmark.
-8 is the number of physical CPU cores present on the machine; 5000000 is the number of bytes allocated per operation.
-8 indicates the benchmark was independently repeated 8 times for statistical averaging; 5000000 is the variance measured across those 8 runs.
assessments.explanation: The -N suffix on a benchmark's printed name reflects GOMAXPROCS at the time of the run -- the number of OS threads the Go runtime will use -- not a run count or core count in the sense the distractors suggest. The number immediately after the name (5000000 here) is the final b.N the runner's calibration process settled on before it judged the total elapsed time long enough to be a stable measurement; ns/op is then simply that total elapsed time divided by this b.N. Option A misreads both figures. Option C conflates GOMAXPROCS with physical core count and misattributes the second figure to an allocation statistic that only appears with -benchmem. Option D invents an averaging/variance mechanism that isn't how a single benchmark invocation's reported numbers are produced.

assessments.prompt: Why does the idiomatic benchmarking command use `go test -bench=. -run=^$` rather than just `go test -bench=.` on its own?
options: -bench=. is invalid syntax on its own and always fails to run without an accompanying -run flag.

go test by default also runs every regular TestXxx function in the package even when only benchmarks were requested; -run=^$ is a regular expression matching no test name at all, which skips running the tests so only the requested benchmarks actually execute.
-run=^$ tells go test to run the matched benchmarks in a randomized order instead of their declared source order.
-run=^$ is required to enable the -benchmem flag; without it, allocation statistics are never reported, regardless of -bench.
assessments.explanation: go test -bench=. alone still runs the package's ordinary TestXxx functions in addition to the matched benchmarks, which is often unwanted noise and extra time while specifically iterating on performance. -run takes a regular expression matched against test names, and ^$ (anchored start immediately followed by anchored end) matches no actual test name at all, effectively skipping every TestXxx function while leaving -bench's own matching untouched. Option A is wrong -- -bench=. is valid and runs fine on its own; the issue is what else runs alongside it, not a syntax failure. Option C invents an ordering effect -run=^$ doesn't have. Option D is wrong -- -benchmem is independent of -run and works whether or not tests are also being run.

assessments.prompt: A benchmark runs expensive setup, then calls b.ResetTimer(), then runs its `for i := 0; i < b.N; i++` loop. The runner's calibration process re-runs this entire function multiple times with successively larger b.N values before settling on a final measurement. Does the expensive setup's cost get correctly excluded from the reported measurement on every one of those re-runs, or only the first?
options: Only the first re-run -- b.ResetTimer's effect doesn't persist or reapply on later calibration attempts, so subsequent re-runs incorrectly fold setup cost back into the measurement.

On every re-run -- b.ResetTimer() is simply an ordinary line inside the function body, so it executes fresh (immediately after that same setup call) every single time the whole function runs again during calibration, correctly zeroing out that specific run's accumulated setup cost each time.
Never -- b.ResetTimer only affects the allocation counters (B/op, allocs/op) reported under -benchmem, not elapsed time, so setup time is always folded into ns/op regardless.
Only if b.ResetTimer() is instead called once, before the benchmark function is invoked at all, from a separate TestMain function.
assessments.explanation: Because b.ResetTimer() is just an ordinary statement inside the benchmark function's own body, it runs again, in full, every single time the entire function is re-executed during the runner's calibration process -- there's no separate persistent state to "wear off" between re-runs; each re-run's setup cost gets freshly zeroed out by that same line, right after that re-run's own setup call completes. Option A invents a one-time-only limitation the mechanism doesn't have. Option C is wrong -- ResetTimer zeroes both elapsed time and allocation counters, not just the -benchmem-specific ones. Option D describes an approach (a separate TestMain) that isn't how ResetTimer is meant to be used or how it actually works; it's called directly inside the benchmark function itself, not externally.

assessments.prompt: A teammate benchmarks two implementations of a function and one reports a dramatically, almost impossibly faster ns/op than the other, despite both looking algorithmically similar. Explain the most likely explanation and how to verify it, and separately explain why b.ResetTimer matters for benchmarks with expensive setup.
assessments.modelAnswer: The single most likely explanation for one benchmark reporting an implausibly fast result relative to an algorithmically similar competitor is dead-code elimination: if that benchmark's loop computes a result and never does anything with it -- no assignment to a variable that's read anywhere the compiler can see -- the compiler may determine the computed value is provably unused and skip performing some or all of the actual work needed to produce it, particularly for small functions that get inlined at the call site, which removes the function-call boundary that would otherwise force the compiler to treat the result as opaque. The way to verify this is to check whether the benchmark's result flows anywhere durable -- the standard idiom is to assign the loop's result into a local variable each iteration, then assign that local into a package-level 'sink' variable once after the loop finishes; because the compiler cannot prove nothing outside the function will ever read a package-level variable, it can no longer justify eliminating the work. If restructuring the suspiciously-fast benchmark with a sink pattern makes its reported time jump up to something comparable to the other implementation, that's strong confirmation the original number was measuring little more than an empty loop. Separately, b.ResetTimer solves an entirely different problem: many realistic benchmarks need expensive one-time setup -- building a large dataset, populating a cache -- before the actual per-operation loop can run, and that setup cost has nothing to do with the per-operation performance the benchmark is meant to characterize. Without calling b.ResetTimer immediately after that setup and before the b.N loop, the elapsed time (and allocation counts) from setup get folded into the benchmark's overall measurement, and because the entire benchmark function -- setup included -- may be re-executed multiple times during the runner's calibration process, that setup cost gets paid, and counted, repeatedly. b.ResetTimer zeroes out everything accumulated so far at the point it's called, so the final reported ns/op reflects only the cost of the loop's own operations, giving a measurement that's actually about the thing you intended to measure rather than being dominated by unrelated setup overhead.
